claims.text: Interfacial interactions govern the high-temperature structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Interfacial interactions dominate over intrinsic configurational entropy in determining nanoalloy stability.
Supportive or passivating layers provide stabilizing interfacial interactions.
These interfacial interactions retard surface diffusion at high temperature.
These interfacial interactions retard phase segregation at high temperature.
The proposed starting nanoparticles are near-equiatomic, mixed-element high-entropy nanoalloys with initially uniform phases.
The controlled comparison varies the interfacial environment among free-standing particles, defect-rich-carbon-supported particles, and inert-oxide-supported particles.
The proposed thermal exposure is 800–1200 °C under otherwise identical atmospheric and pressure conditions.
Nanoalloy-support bonding modulates surface-diffusion pathways.
The support interface acts as a barrier to atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses the nucleation of phase segregation or elemental de-mixing.
Unsupported nanoalloys allow thermal energy to activate surface diffusion and chemical de-mixing more readily than supported nanoalloys.
Supported nanoalloys will show less surface diffusion than free-standing nanoalloys after identical thermal exposure.
Supported nanoalloys will show less elemental segregation and a more uniform chemical distribution than free-standing nanoalloys.
Supported nanoalloys will undergo less pronounced structural change than free-standing nanoalloys.
The prediction is bounded to particles of similar composition and size, temperatures of 800–1200 °C, and experiments in which support nature is the only varied factor.
Reactive atmospheres may change the predicted support effect.
The magnitude of stabilization may depend on support porosity, defect density, and detailed interfacial structure.
TEM-EDS, XRD, and high-resolution imaging can be used to compare chemical segregation, phase changes, and defects after heat treatment.
A lack of a statistically significant difference in segregation and surface diffusion between supported and free-standing particles is designated as a falsifying outcome.
